title: EDUCATION: Forgetting Is a Prerequisite for Memory
author: Eva Keiffenheim
summary: Eva Keiffenheim argues that effective learning feels uncomfortable, not smooth, because the brain mechanisms that produce durable retention differ from those that produce momentary fluency. Drawing on Robert and Elizabeth Bjork's distinction between retrieval strength (how easily something is accessed right now) and storage strength (how durably it is retained), she shows that common habits like re-reading, highlighting, and watching clear explanations create false fluency -- a sense of understanding that evaporates when support is removed. She presents four evidence-backed learning truths: effort strengthens memory, forgetting is part of learning (spaced repetition works precisely when recall feels difficult), productive boredom deepens focus, and early failure prepares the brain for deeper understanding when instruction follows. AI tools amplify the fluency illusion by providing instant polished answers; research shows students who use AI freely during practice often score worse later when AI is unavailable. The practical recommendation: try first, struggle a bit, then use AI to check, correct, or expand -- not to replace the initial struggle.
points: Bjork retrieval/storage strength distinction: high retrieval strength right now does not equal durable storage strength later -- fluency is misleading.
Re-reading, highlighting, and watching clear explanations are recognition activities, not learning activities; they strengthen familiarity, not recall.
Four desirable difficulties: retrieval practice, spaced repetition, productive boredom, and pre-instruction struggle all feel uncomfortable but build lasting memory.
AI amplifies the fluency illusion -- students who use AI freely during practice perform worse later when AI is removed.
Productive failure research (53 studies, Manu Kapur): struggling with a problem before instruction deepens conceptual understanding more than instruction-first approaches.
quotes: Psychologists Robert and Elizabeth Bjork describe this as the difference between retrieval strength and storage strength. Retrieval strength is how easily you can access something right now. Storage strength is how well it is actually learned and retained over time.

Re-reading a page feels familiar, so it seems like you know it. Watching a clear explanation feels like understanding, but the speaker is carrying the thinking. Even polished AI answers can give the illusion that you've mastered something, when you've only recognized it.
The problem isn't that you forget. It's that you expect not to.
Struggle only helps if it's at the right level. If something is so hard that you have no idea where to start, your working memory gets overloaded and learning breaks down.
Learning happens when you engage with what you can't yet do or recall. That process often feels uncertain or uncomfortable.
